newsitem.title: UK: British August car sales seen at near-record high.
newsitem.headline: British August car sales seen at near-record high.

text.p: Britain's motor industry expects August car sales will race to a near-record high of 490,000 cars as drivers rush to get hold of the new 'R' registration prefix, likely to make history by becoming the last to be annually updated.

The new 'R' number-plated cars are available from August 1 and reservations indicate sales for the month will be second only to the all-time high of 500,112 cars sold in 1989 before Britain's last consumer boom turned to bust.
If the August car sales hit 490,000 cars, as anticipated, the industry says it could pass the 2.1 million sales level by the end of the year.

Windfall payments from building societies converting into banks have fuelled demand this year, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT), the industry group which monitors the car sales figures.

Richard Bennett, media manager at the SMMT said the 'R' registration was widely expected to be the last to be annually updated as the industry awaits for a government decision on proposals to change the system.

"We anticipate a change anytime now," Barrett told Reuters. "We are calling for the registration to be changed twice a year, probably March and September, and the government should prove receptive. Ministers could give us an answer in the next few days."
The car industry has fought fiercely for a change to the annual registration system, complaining that the existing set-up is hugely bureaucratic and expensive for the industry.
The SMMT said in a recent statement: "It doesn't work. One change of letter per year puts huge pressure on the manufacturers to produce a huge slice of the total year's output for one month.
"This knocks on to suppliers...and ultimately to the dealers who have a storage nightmare for August 1st."
Around one quarter of total annual car sales are made in August as status-conscious drivers scramble to secure the first new number plated cars.
"The industry is very busy for a few months and very quiet for the rest," said Barrett. "We'd like to smooth out that process."
The Department of Transport (DOT) refused to comment on when a decision on the registration issue would be made.
"At the moment the results of the consultation paper are being considered by ministers. We are still waiting for a decision and we have no fixed date," said the DOT spokeswoman.
The consultation paper was published last December.
